kf1.tip: Choose a story you heard second-hand, such as a school rumour, and explain how schemas and effort after meaning could change it in each retelling.
kf1.note: A good answer names a real second-hand story and traces it through more than one retelling. It must show schemas at work: each teller fills gaps with what they expect to be true, so odd details are dropped or swapped for familiar ones. It must also show effort after meaning: the story becomes more logical and coherent, even if that means changing it. If your story only gets longer or more exciting, link each change back to expectation.

kf2.tip: Imagine Bartlett had given his British participants a familiar British folk tale instead of The War of the Ghosts. Say what would follow for his results and conclusion.
kf2.note: A strong answer sees that a familiar tale would already fit participants' schemas. So there would be fewer gaps to fill and fewer foreign elements to omit or rationalise. Changes would be harder to spot, and the study could not show so clearly that schemas distort memory. Most would conclude the evidence for reconstruction would look much weaker. The trap is saying memory would become a faithful replay, rather than saying the design would reveal less.

cs1.tip: Make the strongest case for and against the claim that the War of the Ghosts study is too loosely controlled to trust, then decide which side wins.
cs1.note: A strong answer weighs three things. The story was not standardised in all versions. Bartlett used no statistical analysis, only qualitative descriptions, so the study is hard to replicate and general conclusions are limited. Against this, recalling a meaningful story has ecological validity, and repeated recall shows change over time. Most decide the claim is partly right: the findings are useful but shaky. The trap is listing both sides without deciding.
